summary: Defines MIB objects for managing the configuration, monitoring and control of Physical Units and Logical Units in an SNA environment, using SMIv2. It replaced RFC 1665. It is historic.

eli5.summary: Gauges for checking parts of an older IBM network. It replaced an earlier version and is now historic.

subtitle: An SNMPv2 MIB for configuring and monitoring IBM SNA nodes, logical units and their sessions.

tldr.problem: SNA networks have Physical Units and Logical Units that operators needed to configure, monitor and control through the same SNMP tools used for TCP/IP gear.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the SNANAU MIB module in SMIv2, with snaNode, snaLu and snaMgtTools groups. Paired Admin and Oper tables separate what a management station asks for from what the SNA system is actually doing.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1666 obsoletes RFC 1665 and is now Historic, so it is a record of an older approach rather than a current standard.

today: RFC 1666 is Historic. It obsoleted RFC 1665, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the SNANAU MIB Manages
sections.content:
RFC 1666 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing Physical Units (PUs) and Logical Units (LUs) in an SNA environment. Both are kinds of Network Addressable Units (NAUs), the origination or destination points for SNA data streams. The objects cover configuration, monitoring and control.

The memo covers PU Type 1.0, 2.0 and 2.1 and LU Type 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7. The generic objects can also manage LU 6.2 and any LU-LU session, but only objects common to all PU and LU types are included. LU 6.2 specific objects are not in this module. It obsoletes RFC 1665 and was published as a Standards Track document in August 1994.
sections.eli5: Some old company networks had many kinds of machines and sessions between them. This document lists the settings and readings that a manager's tool can use for them.

sections.title: The SNMPv2 Framework It Builds On
sections.content:
The memo sits inside the SNMPv2 Network Management Framework, which has four parts: the SMI in RFC 1442 (how objects are described and named), MIB-II in RFC 1213 (core objects for the Internet suite), the administrative model in RFC 1445, and the protocol operations in RFC 1448.

Objects are defined using a subset of ASN.1. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and the object type plus an instance identifies one specific instantiation. The module uses the TimeStamp textual convention from RFC 1443, which holds the value of MIB-II's sysUpTime when something happens. sysUpTime is a clock in the SNMP agent or proxy agent, counted in hundredths of a second.
sections.eli5: The rules for writing down every dial and gauge already existed. This document just uses them to describe the dials and gauges for SNA.

sections.title: Groups, Admin Tables and Oper Tables
sections.content:
The module has three groups: snaNode (node configuration, monitoring and control), snaLu (LU definition, monitoring and control) and snaMgtTools (objects for management tools well known in SNA). The module is registered as { mib-2 34 }.

Objects are organized into two kinds of table. An Admin table holds parameters a management station uses to affect the SNA service; some set up the next startup and others take effect immediately. An Oper table augments the matching Admin table and holds the values the SNA system is using right now. A management station cannot modify Oper entries, and an agent creates a node's Oper row once the Admin entry becomes active.

The snaNode group includes the node admin and oper tables, a statistics table for PU 2.0, and node link admin and oper tables that tie a node to one or more links. The snaLu group includes LU admin and oper tables, a session table and a session statistics table. The optional snaMgtTools group has one table, snaLuRtmTable, with Response Time Monitor variables for LU 2 entries.

Four traps are defined: node state change, node activation failure (failure of ACTPU received from the host), LU state change and LU session BIND failure.
sections.eli5: Each thing has two cards. One card is what you asked for, and you can change it. The other is what is really happening, and you can only read it.

sections.title: Creating Rows and Changing State
sections.content:
A management station can create and delete nodes and LUs through the RowStatus objects in snaNodeAdminTable and snaLuAdminTable, and create or delete node-to-link entries through snaNodeLinkAdminTable. Before an agent accepts the destroy value for an entry, it has to check the operational state of the matching Oper entry.

A node is activated or deactivated with the snaNodeAdminState object, which takes inactive (1) or active (2). The node's operational state, snaNodeOperState, can be inactive, active, waiting or stopping. A new node starts as inactive and the agent accepts no operations for it until its RowStatus is active. A session can be deactivated through the AdminState object in snaLuSessnTable, and when a session goes to unbound the agent removes its row.

The MIB does not support creating links, activating or deactivating LUs, or activating sessions.
sections.eli5: You can add a new machine to the list by adding a row, and you can switch a machine on or off. The panel will not let you start a chat between two machines or make a new cable.

sections.title: Conformance and Security
sections.content:
Conformance is defined by groups. snaNodeGroup, snaLuGroup and snaSessionGroup are mandatory. snaPu20Group is mandatory only for entities that implement PU type 2.0, and snaMgtToolsRtmGroup only for entities that implement LU type 2 and RTM. An agent that does not implement row creation must at least support modification requests, with read-write access instead of read-create.

The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.eli5: Some parts of the panel are required and some only matter if you own the matching machine. The document does not talk about keeping the panel safe.
